# Rules of the air

> The sky has no STOP signs, but it does have strict rules. To avoid collisions you need to know SERA inside out.
>
>
> In this chapter you will learn:
>
>
> * The SERA regulation, the European highway code of the air.
> * The “see and avoid” principle of visual flight (VFR).
> * Who gives way to whom (balloons > gliders > powered aircraft).
> * When you may fly low (ridges, field landings), and when you may not.

## The highway code of the sky: SERA

In Europe we all fly under one regulation: **SERA** (**Standardised European Rules of the Air**). As an EU regulation it applies directly in Spain, and Real Decreto 1180/2018 (Royal Decree 1180/2018) implements it in detail. Whether you fly in Albacete or in Germany, the basic rules are the same.

The underlying principle is **VFR** (**Visual Flight Rules**): we fly by looking outside.

## Basic principle: “see and avoid”

In visual flight, avoiding collisions is your job. Air traffic control (ATC) can help, but the final responsibility is yours. That means scanning the sky all the time (the visual scanning technique) and doing a little gymnastics: blind spots are real, so move the aircraft or your head to see behind the canopy frame and under the nose.

::: {.callout-warning title="Safety"}
Most collisions happen on clear days and close to aerodromes. Never assume the other pilot has seen you. If in doubt, give way.
:::

## Right of way

Who goes first when two aircraft meet? SERA.3210 settles it.

### 1. The manoeuvrability hierarchy

When two aircraft are **converging** (crossing tracks at roughly the same level), SERA gives priority to the one that can manoeuvre least:

1. **Balloons**: highest priority; they can hardly manoeuvre.
2. **Gliders**: we can only go down, and we cannot hold level indefinitely.
3. **Airships**.
4. **Powered aeroplanes and microlights**: they have an engine and manoeuvre at will.

There is one exception: powered aircraft must give way to aircraft towing other aircraft or objects (a banner, or the tug-glider combination itself), because a tow combination manoeuvres far less freely. The rule does not bind you as a free-flying glider, but common sense does: keep clear of an aerotow combination as soon as you see it.

Careful: this hierarchy only decides when converging. Head-on and when overtaking, category does not count, and any aircraft gives way to one whose manoeuvrability is impaired or that is compelled to land (SERA.3210(b) and (c)(4)).

### 2. Conflict situations

* **Head-on**: both turn to their **right**.

* **Converging**: on crossing tracks at the same level, the one coming from the **right** has priority. Careful: if you are coming from the right under power and the other aircraft is a glider, the hierarchy wins and the glider has priority.
* **Overtaking**: if you catch up with another aircraft from behind, the one ahead has priority. Overtake it on its **right**. There is one exception made for us: a glider overtaking another glider may pass **on the right or on the left** (useful on a ridge, where only one side is safe).
* **On a ridge**: if two gliders meet on a collision course while ridge soaring, **the one with the hill on its right has priority**. The other must turn away from the slope to give way (@fig-01-cap05-prioridades-ladera). This rule **is not in SERA**: it is a convention that glider pilots follow everywhere. The regulation's head-on rule has *both* aircraft turn right, which is impossible for the one with the slope on that side.

![Right of way when ridge soaring](imagenes/01-cap05-preferencias-paso-ladera.jpeg){#fig-01-cap05-prioridades-ladera}

* **Landing**: the lowest glider has priority to land (but you may not dive to cut in). Under SERA.3210, gliders on final and landing also always have priority over powered aircraft (@fig-01-cap05-prioridades).

![Right-of-way rules: three encounters between gliders, each with its avoiding manoeuvre. *(FIX: the panels are unlabelled and the arrows do not make each glider's heading clear; the rule for each situation is in the text.)*](imagenes/01-cap05-prioridades-paso.jpg){#fig-01-cap05-prioridades .corregir}

## Minimum flight heights

SERA.5005 sets minimum heights to protect people and property on the ground. Except when taking off or landing, you may not fly below:

1. **300 m** above the highest obstacle within a radius of 600 m, when flying over congested areas (cities, towns, gatherings of people).
2. **150 m** above ground or water, or above the highest obstacle within a radius of 150 m, anywhere else (@fig-01-cap05-alturas-minimas).

### Exceptions for gliding

SERA.5005(f) allows exceptions “by permission from the competent authority”, and its AMC1 leaves it to that same authority to set the minimum heights for ridge soaring and forced landing practice. In Spain they are set by **article 33 of Real Decreto 1180/2018**, which repealed Real Decreto 552/2014. Article 33 (unofficial translation) allows flight below the heights in SERA.5005(f)(2) (the 150 m in open country, not the 300 m over populated areas) in two cases that matter to us:

* **Ridge soaring**: gliders flying on ridges are exempt, provided they create no risk or nuisance to persons or property on the surface.
* **Forced landing training**: you may descend to **50 m** (the rule says “50 m (150 ft)”, although 50 m is about 164 ft), provided there is no risk or nuisance to persons or property on the surface, keeping 150 m from any person, vehicle or vessel on the surface and from any artificial obstacle, and meeting the conditions of the operator's safety study: that of your school or club.

![Minimum safe heights. *(FIX: in the ridge-soaring panel the glider must be on the windward slope, where the air rises, not on the lee side; and the 300 m over the city are measured from the highest obstacle, not from a low rooftop.)*](imagenes/01-cap05-alturas-minimas.jpg){#fig-01-cap05-alturas-minimas .corregir}

::: {.callout-tip title="Golden rule"}
**When converging: balloon > glider > airship > powered.**
Head-on, both to the right (on a ridge, the convention). If you are overtaking, you keep clear.
Landing aircraft go first.
:::

::: {.postit}
**Chapter summary: rules of the air**

The **SERA** regulation is the highway code of the sky:

* **VFR**: we fly to see and be seen. Eyes outside.
* **Right of way**: when converging, balloons > gliders > powered (the one that can manoeuvre most gives way) and, between equals, the one coming from the right has priority. Head-on, both turn right; the overtaking aircraft keeps clear, whatever its category. When landing, the lowest glider goes first, and gliders have priority over powered aircraft. On a ridge, the one with the hill on its right has priority: a gliding convention, not a SERA rule.
* **Minimum heights (SERA.5005(f))**: 150 m above the ground or the highest obstacle within a radius of 150 m; 300 m over populated areas. In Spain, Real Decreto 1180/2018 (art. 33) exempts gliders on a ridge from the 150 m, provided there is no risk or nuisance to persons or property, and allows descent to 50 m when practising forced landings, 150 m from any person, vehicle or vessel and from any artificial obstacle, and in line with the operator's safety study.
:::
